rules.title: ITAR "U.S. Person" Definition
rules.summary: Under ITAR (22 CFR 120.62), a "U.S. person" is a U.S. citizen, a lawful permanent resident (green card holder), or a "protected individual" under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) (which also covers certain asylees/refugees who timely pursue naturalization). Anyone else — including H-1B, L-1, O-1, F-1/OPT, J-1, and TN visa holders — is a "foreign person" under 22 CFR 120.63, no matter how long they've lived or worked in the U.S. Most defense-tech roles touching USML-controlled technical data require the worker to be a U.S. person, or the employer to hold a specific DDTC license/exemption for that individual. This is strictly an export-control test, and it is NOT the test for a security clearance. Clearances are limited to U.S. citizens (Executive Order 12968 § 3.1(b); 32 CFR 117.10(k)): a green card holder is a U.S. person here but still a non-U.S. citizen for clearance purposes, eligible at most for a rare, contract-specific Limited Access Authorization that is never valid for TOP SECRET (see clearance-citizenship and laa-non-citizen). So a green card opens ITAR-only roles, but not roles that require a clearance.
keyPoints: U.S. person = citizen, green card holder (LPR), or certain protected asylees/refugees (8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3))
Does NOT include H-1B, L-1, O-1, F-1/OPT, J-1, TN, or any other non-immigrant visa holder
Green card holders qualify directly as "lawful permanent resident" (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(20)) — no naturalization-timing condition attached to that prong
Asylees/refugees without a green card qualify only if they applied for naturalization within the timeframes 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) requires
A company can still employ foreign persons under a specific DDTC license or exemption, but that's the exception, not the default

This is about ITAR access only. A security clearance has a different, stricter test — U.S. citizenship — so green card holders, though U.S. persons here, cannot hold a regular clearance; the only exception is a rare Limited Access Authorization, never valid for TOP SECRET (see clearance-citizenship)

rules.title: Security Clearances Require U.S. Citizenship: a Green Card Is Not Enough
rules.summary: A U.S. security clearance is open to U.S. citizens. Executive Order 12968 § 3.1(b) says eligibility for access to classified information "shall be granted only to employees who are United States citizens," with narrow exceptions, and 32 CFR 117.10(k) tells contractors to "make every effort to ensure that non-U.S. citizens are not employed in duties that may require access to classified information." This is where green card holders most often get bad advice: a green card makes you a "U.S. person" under ITAR (22 CFR 120.62), which opens ITAR-only roles, but it does not make you eligible for a clearance. The only exception for any non-citizen is a Limited Access Authorization (see laa-non-citizen): granted in "rare circumstances" for skills urgently needed on a specific government contract when no cleared or clearable U.S. citizen is available, approved by a government senior official, never valid for TOP SECRET, and never granted on a temporary (interim) basis. In practice: if a posting requires a clearance — including "eligible to obtain" one — a green card holder should expect not to qualify; if it requires only U.S.-person status under ITAR, they do.
keyPoints: Clearance eligibility is for U.S. citizens (EO 12968 § 3.1(b)); contractors must make every effort to keep non-U.S. citizens out of duties needing classified access (32 CFR 117.10(k))
A green card makes you a U.S. person under ITAR (22 CFR 120.62) — enough for ITAR-only roles, not for a clearance

Non-U.S. citizens are never eligible for temporary (interim) access (32 CFR 117.10(l))
"Eligible to obtain a clearance" in a posting therefore includes U.S. citizenship
Becoming a U.S. citizen is what makes a green card holder clearance-eligible — the green card alone does not

rules.title: Limited Access Authorization (LAA) for Non-U.S. Citizens
rules.summary: A Limited Access Authorization (LAA) is a separate, much stricter pathway than ITAR's "U.S. person" test (see itar-us-person) for a non-U.S. citizen to access U.S. classified information, under 32 CFR § 117.10(k). It is capped at SECRET — never TOP SECRET, Restricted Data/Formerly Restricted Data, COMSEC information, intelligence information, or (except for NATO-member nationals under specific conditions) NATO information. A Cognizant Security Agency may only grant one in "rare circumstances": the individual has specialized skills urgently needed for a specific U.S. Government contract AND a cleared or clearable U.S. citizen is not readily available, approved by a Government Contracting Activity senior official — it is not a general clearance and does not transfer between contracts. It applies to every non-U.S. citizen, green card holders included: Executive Order 12968 § 2.6 names "immigrant alien and foreign national employees" explicitly, and being a U.S. person under ITAR (see itar-us-person) does not change this (see clearance-citizenship). Non-U.S. citizens are also never eligible for temporary (interim) access (32 CFR 117.10(l)).
keyPoints: Capped at SECRET — never TOP SECRET, Restricted Data/Formerly Restricted Data, COMSEC information, intelligence information, or (except NATO-member nationals under specific conditions) NATO information (32 CFR § 117.10(k))
Granted only in "rare circumstances": specialized skills urgently needed for a specific U.S. Government contract, and a cleared or clearable U.S. citizen is not readily available
Requires approval from a Government Contracting Activity senior official — not an automatic or routine determination
Scoped to the specific contract/program that justified it, not a general-purpose clearance

Applies to every non-U.S. citizen, green card holders included (EO 12968 § 2.6: "immigrant alien and foreign national employees") — ITAR "U.S. person" status (see itar-us-person) exempts no one from it
Non-U.S. citizens are never eligible for temporary (interim) access to classified information (32 CFR 117.10(l))

rules.title: EAR "Deemed Export" vs. ITAR
rules.summary: Under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR, 15 CFR 734.13), releasing controlled "technology" or source code to a foreign person inside the U.S. is legally treated as an export to that person's country of citizenship or permanent residency — a "deemed export." EAR is administered by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a separate regime from ITAR's DDTC/State Department. Practically, EAR is more graduated than ITAR: it exempts U.S. dual citizens and green card holders outright, and allows case-by-case deemed-export licenses for other foreign nationals depending on their specific nationality and the technology involved. ITAR has no equivalent per-nationality licensing path for most defense articles — it is close to a binary U.S.-person/foreign-person test instead. For an engineering job: if the work touches USML-controlled defense technical data, expect an essentially all-U.S.-persons team; if it's "dual-use" tech controlled only under EAR, a foreign-national teammate may be workable with the right export license.
keyPoints: Deemed export = releasing controlled technology or source code to a foreign person inside the U.S., treated as an export to their home country (15 CFR 734.13(b))
Administered by BIS/Commerce (EAR) — a distinct regime from DDTC/State (ITAR)
EAR explicitly exempts U.S. dual citizens and green card holders from deemed-export treatment
EAR licensing can be nationality-specific and case-by-case; ITAR generally cannot — ITAR is closer to all-or-nothing U.S.-person access
Which regime applies depends on whether the specific technology is on the USML (ITAR) or is dual-use/EAR-only

rules.title: SF-86 and the eApp Filing System
rules.summary: The SF-86 ("Questionnaire for National Security Positions") is the core background-investigation form behind any security clearance, and it is filed electronically, not on paper. The legacy e-QIP filing portal has been replaced by "eApp," and the underlying form itself is also changing: DCSA began an internal rollout of a new, consolidated "Personnel Vetting Questionnaire" (PVQ) in April 2026, intended to eventually replace the SF-86/SF-85/SF-85P forms outright. Only the updated (February 2024 edition) SF-86 filed through eApp has been accepted since mid-2025; older/legacy-form submissions stopped being accepted August 1, 2025. Candidates fill this out themselves once sponsored by an employer — it covers 10+ years of history, foreign contacts, and finances, and should never be filled out by, or shared with, a third party.

rules.title: NBIS vs. DISS: Current System of Record
rules.summary: DISS (Defense Information System for Security) replaced the older JPAS as the system of record in 2021. The National Background Investigation Services (NBIS) program was meant to eventually replace DISS entirely, but as of November 2026 that full cutover has not happened — DCSA has actually pulled key case-management functions back toward an upgraded DISS. Industry case-initiation and review ("IRA") functionality moved into "DISS-JVS" on July 31, 2026; September 30, 2026 was the last day to start new cases in "NBIS-Agency"; and NBIS-Agency becomes fully read-only after November 30, 2026, with any unfinished case needing to be re-started in DISS-JVS. In short: DISS-JVS, not NBIS, is the live day-to-day system right now. Either way, access to these systems is restricted to vetted Facility Security Officers — individual candidates and recruiters cannot query them directly, which is exactly why self-attestation plus FSO verification at offer stage remain the only legitimate path.
keyPoints: JPAS → DISS transition completed in 2021
NBIS was meant to replace DISS, but as of Nov 2026 that full replacement has not happened
DCSA is moving case-initiation/review functions back into an upgraded "DISS-JVS," not forward into NBIS
Key 2026 dates: DISS-JVS industry go-live July 31; last NBIS-Agency case-initiation Sept 30; NBIS-Agency read-only after Nov 30
Only FSOs can query DISS/NBIS/Scattered Castles — there is no way for a candidate or recruiter to self-verify a clearance in these systems

rules.title: SEAD 4: The 13 Adjudicative Guidelines
rules.summary: Security Executive Agent Directive 4 (signed by the Director of National Intelligence in December 2016, effective June 8, 2017) sets the single, government-wide set of criteria every agency uses to decide whether to grant or keep someone's security clearance eligibility. It defines 13 guidelines, lettered A through M, each evaluated together under a "whole person" concept — no single factor is automatically disqualifying, and every guideline lists both disqualifying and mitigating conditions. No superseding revision of SEAD 4 was found as of this research date; it remains the current, controlling version.
keyPoints: A — Allegiance to the United States
B — Foreign Influence
C — Foreign Preference
D — Sexual Behavior
E — Personal Conduct
F — Financial Considerations
G — Alcohol Consumption
H — Drug Involvement and Substance Misuse
I — Psychological Conditions
J — Criminal Conduct
K — Handling Protected Information
L — Outside Activities
M — Use of Information Technology

rules.title: SEAD 7: Clearance Reciprocity
rules.summary: Security Executive Agent Directive 7 (November 9, 2018) requires federal agencies to accept another authorized agency's existing background investigation and clearance-eligibility determination at the same or higher level, instead of re-investigating someone from scratch, as long as the investigation is still within scope. For industry/contractor employees specifically, this duty is implemented through 32 CFR 117.10 (the NISPOM rule). Reciprocity generally holds when the underlying investigation is current with no new derogatory information, and, for DoD, when there has been no break in service of more than 24 months (32 CFR 156.5(h)(3) — the 24-month rule comes from there, not from SEAD 7, which addresses investigations more than seven years old case by case). SEAD 7 directs agencies to make a reciprocity determination within five business days of receiving the request, a deadline for that one step rather than an end-to-end time. Only the Security Executive Agent (the DNI) may generally disallow reciprocal recognition, and only for specific national-security reasons.
keyPoints: Agencies must accept another authorized agency's clearance eligibility at the same or higher level

Reciprocity generally applies when the prior investigation is current with no new adverse information; for DoD, a break in service of more than 24 months ends it (32 CFR 156.5(h)(3)), and SEAD 7 lets agencies accept an investigation more than seven years old case by case
A reciprocity determination on a still-valid case is supposed to be made within about 5 business days
For NISP/contractor personnel, reciprocity is implemented via 32 CFR 117.10
Only the Security Executive Agent (DNI) can generally disallow reciprocal recognition, for specific national-security reasons

rules.title: Continuous Vetting (Trusted Workforce 2.0)
rules.summary: Continuous Vetting (CV) replaces the old model of one deep reinvestigation every 5-10 years with ongoing, automated record checks (criminal, terrorism, financial, public records, foreign travel, and more) that generate alerts for a human adjudicator to review as they occur. It is the centerpiece of the government's "Trusted Workforce 2.0" reform. As of the end of June 2026, DCSA formally retired legacy periodic reinvestigations for the national-security workforce (with only limited exceptions), making CV the default; the broader federal "public trust" population is still being enrolled (about 54% as of mid-2026, expected substantially complete by the end of 2026). Day to day, a cleared person generally no longer faces one big reinvestigation case every several years — instead they are expected to self-report qualifying life events between automated checks, and an alert can trigger a review at any time rather than only on a fixed schedule.
keyPoints: Replaces periodic reinvestigation (previously every 5 years for TS/SCI, 5-10 years for Secret) with ongoing automated checks
Legacy periodic reinvestigations for the national-security population were formally retired at the end of June 2026

NISP contractor personnel now get a simplified questionnaire every 5 years instead of a full reinvestigation case (announced May 19, 2026)

rules.title: Interim (Temporary) Clearance Eligibility
rules.summary: An interim — officially "temporary" — eligibility determination lets someone start working at the Top Secret, Secret, or Confidential level before their full investigation and final adjudication are complete, based on preliminary checks showing no disqualifying information so far. It does not cover Restricted Data, COMSEC, or NATO classified information, which always require a final determination, and SCI/Special Access Program access on an interim basis is discretionary and decided case by case. Only U.S. citizens can receive temporary eligibility, and by regulation (32 CFR 117.10) it cannot last more than one year without specific extension approval. It is fully revocable if the completed investigation turns up a problem.
keyPoints: Covers Top Secret/Secret/Confidential collateral work only — not RD, COMSEC, or NATO information
SCI/SAP access on an interim basis is case-by-case, not automatic
Only U.S. citizens are eligible for temporary/interim eligibility
Capped at one year by regulation (32 CFR 117.10) absent specific approval to extend
Fully revocable — it is a preliminary determination, not a guarantee

rules.title: Facility Clearance (FCL) Sponsorship for a New Company
rules.summary: A Facility Clearance (FCL) lets a specific company location store, access, or work with classified information, and a company cannot apply for one on its own — it must be sponsored, either by a government contracting activity with a classified contract for that company or by an already-cleared prime contractor that needs to subcontract classified work to it. The sponsor submits a request through DCSA's National Industrial Security System, typically including a DD Form 254 and a sponsorship letter; DCSA's Facility Clearance Branch then reviews it, and if accepted, the company generally has about 20 days to return required paperwork once DCSA's processing clock starts. The government funds DCSA's own FCL processing; the company's real cost is building out compliant security processes and designating a Facility Security Officer (FSO) beforehand. For an early-stage startup with no FCL yet, the first real bottleneck is usually finding a willing sponsor, not DCSA's internal processing — and packages are often sent back for fixable errors (DCSA's own FCL roadmap lists the top rejection reasons, such as a missing government contracting activity authorization), which adds time. No primary source publishes a typical end-to-end FCL duration.
keyPoints: A company cannot self-apply for an FCL — it must be sponsored by a government contracting activity or an already-cleared prime contractor
Sponsorship request goes through DCSA's NISS, usually with a DD Form 254 and a sponsorship letter
The company should designate a Facility Security Officer (FSO) before or at sponsorship
No government fee for FCL processing itself — the company's cost is internal compliance and FSO time
Packages are often returned for fixable errors — DCSA's FCL roadmap lists the top rejection reasons — so a clean first submission saves real time

rules.title: Current DCSA Clearance Timeliness (FY2026 Q3)
rules.summary: DCSA's own FY2026 Q3 industry figures, presented at the September 2, 2026 NISPPAC public meeting, show an initial Top Secret clearance for industry averaging 243 days end-to-end (20 days initiation + 97 days investigation + 126 days adjudication), and an initial Secret clearance averaging 197 days end-to-end (21 + 59 + 117). These figures have moved a great deal over the past two years: the investigation phase itself has gotten much faster (Top Secret investigation time fell from 234 days a year earlier to 97 days), but the adjudication phase has gotten slower by nearly as much (40 to 126 days for Top Secret over the same period), so the end-to-end total improved far less than the investigation phase alone (Top Secret: 293 days four quarters ago, 243 now — down 50 year over year, though up 22 from last quarter). A separate (not industry-specific) measure from the Performance Accountability Council shows the investigation phase alone averaging 57 days for Moderate-Risk-tier cases (which include Secret) and 82 days for High-Risk-tier cases (which include Top Secret) across 100% of cases in the same quarter, consistent with the industry figures once the investigation step is isolated.
keyPoints: Initial TS (industry), FY2026 Q3: ~243 days end-to-end (20 initiate + 97 investigate + 126 adjudicate)
Initial Secret (industry), FY2026 Q3: ~197 days end-to-end (21 initiate + 59 investigate + 117 adjudicate)
Investigation time has dropped sharply since FY2024-2025; adjudication time has risen just as sharply — that is the current bottleneck
These are DCSA's own published figures (NISPPAC meeting, Sept. 2026), not a stale historical estimate
Figures move quarter to quarter; treat as a snapshot and check for a newer NISPPAC/DCSA release before relying on them long-term

rules.title: Zero-Knowledge Passport Proofs (Self, zkPassport)
rules.summary: Self Protocol and zkPassport are open-source systems that let someone scan their passport, national ID, or similar chip-based document with their phone and generate a zero-knowledge proof of a specific fact — like being over 18, a citizen of a given country, a unique human, or not on a sanctions list — without revealing the underlying document or any other personal data. Both generate the proof on the user's own device and explicitly avoid storing documents or raw data centrally. These are general-purpose identity/humanity tools (built for things like KYC, Sybil-resistant distribution, and age verification) — they have no connection to the U.S. personnel-security-clearance system and cannot prove, and do not claim to prove, that someone holds any level of security clearance.
keyPoints: Both generate zero-knowledge proofs client-side from an NFC passport/ID chip scan
Can prove: age threshold, nationality/citizenship, personhood/uniqueness, sanctions-list status, document validity
Cannot prove, and are not designed to prove, security clearance status or classified-access eligibility
No integration with DISS, NBIS, Scattered Castles, or any DCSA system
The closest thing to a real-world analogy for a future "prove a fact without showing the document" clearance credential — but no such clearance credential exists today

rules.title: W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0 and SD-JWT
rules.summary: W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 became an official, finished W3C Recommendation on May 15, 2025 — the standard web format for cryptographically-signed, tamper-evident digital credentials (comparable to a digital diploma or ID card). It deliberately supports multiple ways of cryptographically "securing" a credential, including SD-JWT. SD-JWT itself (the selective-disclosure mechanism that lets a holder reveal only some fields of a credential) was finalized by the IETF as RFC 9901 in November 2025. A richer profile built on it, "SD-JWT VC," is further along in standardization (draft revision -22 as of October 2026, in IESG review) but is not yet a final RFC. A VC 2.1 maintenance update is already in early draft (April 2026) under a new 2026-2028 working group charter. None of this is specific to clearances — it is general infrastructure for any digital credential.
keyPoints: VC Data Model 2.0 = W3C Recommendation (finished standard) since May 15, 2025
VC 2.0 supports multiple credential-securing mechanisms, including SD-JWT, not just one
Base SD-JWT mechanism = finalized as RFC 9901 (IETF, November 2025)
SD-JWT VC (the verifiable-credential profile) is still an in-progress IETF draft (rev. -22, Oct. 2026), not yet a final RFC
A VC 2.1 maintenance revision is already in First Public Working Draft (April 2026)

rules.title: Mobile Driver's License (mDL) / ISO 18013-5
rules.summary: ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 is the international standard defining how a phone-based mobile driver's license works and how it is presented to a verifier (for example, at an airport security checkpoint); it was approved in August 2021 and remains the currently-published edition, though a second edition is already in development (committee-draft stage as of 2026, not yet published). In the U.S., AAMVA layers additional implementation guidance on top of it for state DMV mDL programs, several states (including California, Colorado, Arizona, and Maryland) have live mDL programs built on it, and TSA's CAT-2 readers at 250+ airport checkpoints already accept an 18013-5-compliant mDL. Like the zero-knowledge passport tools above, this proves identity/age-type facts from a state-issued credential — it has no relationship to security clearance status.

rules.title: Background Checks: the FCRA Sequence
rules.summary: A background check an employer buys from a background-check company (a "consumer reporting agency") is a "consumer report" under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA). Before ordering one, the employer must tell the candidate in writing, in a document that contains only that notice, that a report may be obtained for employment purposes, and must get the candidate's written permission. The employer also certifies to the background-check company that it did both, that it will follow the adverse-action steps if they apply, and that it will not use the report to break equal-employment law. The company sends a summary of the candidate's rights with the report. If the employer may turn the candidate down because of the report, the adverse-action sequence applies (see fcra-adverse-action); when the check may be ordered at all is set by fair-chance laws (see fair-chance-timing).
keyPoints: Before the report is ordered: a clear written notice that a consumer report may be obtained for employment purposes, "in a document that consists solely of the disclosure" (15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(2)(A)(i))

The FTC says the notice cannot be part of the job application; a brief description of what consumer reports are is allowed only if it does not confuse or detract from the notice. In practice, use the background-check company's own notice form rather than adding text to it
Written permission from the candidate, which may be on the same page as the notice; to keep getting reports during employment, the permission must say so clearly (§ 1681b(b)(2)(A)(ii); FTC guidance)

The employer certifies to the background-check company that it gave the notice and got permission, will follow the adverse-action steps if they apply, and will not use the report to violate equal-employment law (§ 1681b(b)(1)(A))
The background-check company supplies "A Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act" with the report (§ 1681b(b)(1)(B))

A reference check done by the background-check company through interviews about a person's character, reputation or way of living is an "investigative consumer report": a separate written notice is due within three days of ordering it, and, if the candidate asks, a written description of the investigation's nature and scope within five days (15 U.S.C. § 1681d(a)-(b))

Arrest records, civil suits and civil judgments older than seven years may not be reported, but that limit does not apply to a job paying, or reasonably expected to pay, $75,000 a year or more (15 U.S.C. § 1681c(a)(2), (b)(3)); convictions are not covered by that limit
Willful violations cost actual damages or $100 to $1,000 per person, plus punitive damages and attorney's fees (15 U.S.C. § 1681n(a))
When the report is no longer needed, dispose of it securely (FTC guidance)

rules.title: Adverse Action After a Background Check
rules.summary: "Adverse action" means any unfavourable employment decision, such as not hiring someone or withdrawing an offer, based in whole or in part on a background-check report. The FCRA sets the order: before acting, give the candidate a copy of the report and the summary of their rights (the "pre-adverse action notice"); wait, so they can point out errors; then, if the decision stands, give the adverse-action notice. The statute names no waiting period. FTC staff said in an informal 1997 opinion that five business days "appears reasonable", and California, New York City and Illinois require at least five business days for decisions based on criminal history (see fair-chance-timing). The duties fall on the employer that takes the action, whoever drafts or sends the letters.
keyPoints: Before acting: give the candidate a copy of the report and a written description of their FCRA rights (15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)(A)); the FTC says this gives the person the chance to review the report and say whether it is correct
Wait: the statute is silent on how long. FTC staff (informal, 1997) said a five-business-day period "appears reasonable", while the facts of a particular situation may require a different time

Then the adverse-action notice (oral, written or electronic): that the action was taken; the background-check company's name, address and phone number; a statement that the company did not make the decision and cannot explain it; the right to a free copy of the report within 60 days and to dispute its accuracy or completeness; and any credit score used (15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a))
For a decision based on criminal history, fair-chance laws add an individual assessment and their own notices and waiting periods (see fair-chance-timing)

Keep the notices and their dates: hiring records must be kept at least one year (29 CFR 1602.14), four years in California (Gov. Code § 12946), and until a discrimination charge is resolved if one is filed

rules.title: Fair-Chance Laws: When Criminal History May Be Checked
rules.summary: Fair-chance ("ban-the-box") laws delay when an employer may ask about or check criminal history, usually until after a conditional offer, and add steps before turning someone down because of a conviction. Coverage differs by place and by employer size. A rule that meets every law summarised here: order the background check only after a conditional offer has been made (and recorded in writing), and before rejecting anyone for criminal history, do an individual assessment, send a preliminary notice with a copy of the report, wait at least five business days for a response (ten days in California if the candidate disputes the report), and then send a final notice.
keyPoints: Federal contractors: a contractor may not ask, orally or in writing, about the criminal history of an applicant for a position related to the contract before extending a conditional offer. This does not apply where law requires the information before an offer, or to a contract that requires the person hired to have access to classified information or sensitive law-enforcement or national-security duties. A first violation brings a written warning; later ones can suspend contract payments (41 U.S.C. § 4714; 10 U.S.C. § 4657 for defense contracts). Whether the implementing FAR clause has been finalised was not confirmed

California (employers with five or more employees): no conviction questions on applications, no background check or internet search for criminal history before a job offer, and no job ads saying "No Felons" or "Must Have Clean Record". Never consider arrests that did not lead to a conviction (with limited exceptions), sealed, dismissed or diverted cases, or convictions more than seven years old. The law does not apply where an employer is required by law to check or restrict (CRD fact sheet, June 2025)

California process: an individualized assessment (nature and gravity of the offence, time passed, the job's duties); a written preliminary notice listing the convictions, with a copy of the report and the right to respond; at least five business days to respond, at least ten days if the candidate challenges the report's accuracy; then a written final decision with any appeal procedure and the right to complain to the Civil Rights Department

New York City (employers with four or more employees): no criminal-history inquiry before a conditional offer, and cases that ended without a conviction are protected at every stage. To withdraw an offer: a Fair Chance Analysis, a written copy of the inquiry and analysis on the Fair Chance Notice, and at least five business days to respond with the position held open. Where another law requires a check before an offer, the employer must still do the analysis, give the notice and wait (NYC Commission on Human Rights)

Illinois: before acting on a conviction, the employer weighs the statute's factors; a preliminary written notice gives the disqualifying convictions and reasoning, a copy of the conviction report and the right to respond; the candidate has at least five business days; the final decision is in writing with any appeal procedure and the right to file a charge with the Department of Human Rights (775 ILCS 5/2-103.1)
Other cities and states (for example Los Angeles, San Francisco, Philadelphia and Washington State) have their own fair-chance laws; they were not checked for this summary

rules.title: Form I-9: Employment Eligibility Verification
rules.summary: Every U.S. employer completes Form I-9 for every person it hires, citizens included, to verify identity and permission to work in the United States. The new employee completes Section 1 at the time of hire, in practice by the first day of work. Within three business days of the hire, the employer examines the documents the employee chooses to present and completes Section 2. The employer keeps the form itself (it is not filed with the government) for three years after the hire or one year after the job ends, whichever is later. The I-9 is not a citizenship check: export-control checks are kept separate from it (see export-determination-after-offer).
keyPoints: Section 1 (employee information and attestation): at the time of hire (8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(i)(A))

Section 2 (employer review): within three business days of the hire, examine the documents (in person, or remotely under the DHS-authorised alternative procedure for employers who qualify) and complete the section; for a job lasting under three business days, at the time of hire (8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(ii)-(iii); USCIS)

The employee chooses which acceptable documents to show: one List A document, or one List B plus one List C. Limiting that choice, asking for more or different documents than needed, or rejecting valid documents that reasonably appear genuine, because of citizenship, immigration status or national origin, is against the law (DOJ fact sheet)
Current edition 01/20/25; the 08/01/23 edition with the 05/31/2027 expiration date may still be used (USCIS)

Keep each form three years after the hire or one year after employment ends, whichever is later, and make it available for government inspection; do not send it to USCIS or ICE (8 CFR 274a.2(b)(2)(i)(A); USCIS)
Do not mark the I-9 with export-control notes or store export-control documents with it (DOJ fact sheet)

rules.title: E-Verify for New Hires
rules.summary: E-Verify is the federal online system that checks Form I-9 information against government records. Two situations make it required that matter for defense-tech hiring: a federal contract that includes FAR clause 52.222-54, and employing a student on a STEM OPT extension. Under the FAR clause the case is created within three business days after the date of hire, so it comes after the hire, not before. A new hire who holds an active U.S. Government security clearance does not need an E-Verify case under the clause. While a mismatch is unresolved, the employer may not take adverse action against the employee because of it. State laws may require E-Verify in other cases; those were not checked here.
keyPoints: Federal contracts with FAR 52.222-54 (Jan 2025): a contractor not yet enrolled enrols within 30 calendar days of the award, and within 90 days of enrolling starts verifying every new hire working in the U.S. within three business days after the date of hire; employees assigned to the contract are verified on their own schedule

Not required under the clause for an employee who holds an active U.S. Government security clearance for access to confidential, secret or top secret information, who was already verified through E-Verify by the contractor, or who holds HSPD-12 credentials (FAR 52.222-54(d))

STEM OPT: the student's employer must be enrolled in E-Verify and in good standing, sign the Form I-983 training plan, and report the student's departure to the school's designated school official within five business days; DHS may visit the worksite (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)(5)-(6), (11))

A mismatch (tentative nonconfirmation) is not a decision: the employer may not terminate, suspend, delay training, withhold or lower pay, or take any other adverse action because of it until it becomes a final nonconfirmation (e-verify.gov)

Create the case after the person is hired: the FAR clause counts its three business days from the date of hire. E-Verify's own user agreement also bars using it to screen applicants; that wording was not re-checked for this summary

rules.title: Conditional Offers and Their Contingencies
rules.summary: A conditional offer is a job offer that depends on conditions being met after it is made, such as a satisfactory background check. The offer is a turning point for timing: fair-chance laws allow a criminal-history check only after one, the ADA allows a medical examination only after one, and for a role that needs classified access on day one the company's Facility Security Officer (FSO) may ask the government to start the clearance before the start date only once the company has committed to the hire in writing and the candidate has accepted in writing. Typical contingencies for defense roles: a satisfactory background check; proof of identity and work authorisation on Form I-9; for export-controlled work, U.S.-person status or any export licence needed; for cleared work, clearance eligibility or verification of an existing clearance by the FSO; and signing the confidentiality and invention-assignment agreement. Contingency wording varies by state; have counsel approve it.
keyPoints: Background check: order it after the conditional offer (see fair-chance-timing and fcra-background-check)

Clearance before the start date: the contractor may submit the request for investigation early only if it has made a written commitment for employment and the candidate has accepted the offer in writing; the commitment must say employment starts within 45 days of eligibility being granted (32 CFR 117.10(f))

Clearance requests are limited to the minimum number of employees needed and "will not be used to establish a cache of cleared employees" (32 CFR 117.10(a)(5)); the government decides eligibility and notifies the company, which must immediately deny access on a denial (117.10(a)(2))

Medical examinations: none before an offer; after an offer the employer may require one and condition the offer on it only if every entering employee in that job category is examined, with the results kept confidential and separate (42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(2)-(3))
Form I-9: Section 2 is due within three business days of the hire (8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(ii)); see form-i9

Export-controlled work: releasing controlled technical data to a foreign person inside the U.S. is an export (22 CFR 120.50(a)(2)), so the contingency is U.S.-person status or the needed licence before access, not U.S. citizenship (see export-determination-after-offer)

rules.title: Confidentiality and Invention-Assignment Agreements
rules.summary: New hires at technology companies usually sign an agreement that protects confidential information and assigns inventions to the company (often called an NDA or PIIA). Two notices matter. Under federal law, an agreement that governs trade secrets or confidential information must include notice of the whistleblower immunity in the Defend Trade Secrets Act, or the company cannot recover exemplary damages or attorney's fees from that employee. In California, an invention-assignment clause cannot reach an invention made entirely on the employee's own time without the company's equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secrets, unless it relates to the company's business or research or comes from the employee's work, and the employer must give written notice of that limit when the agreement is signed. None of this is the SF 312, the classified-information nondisclosure agreement a cleared employee signs with the government.
keyPoints: Defend Trade Secrets Act: the employer must give notice of the whistleblower immunity in any contract with an employee that governs trade secrets or confidential information; a cross-reference to a policy document that sets out the reporting policy also counts; without it, no exemplary damages or attorney's fees against that employee (18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3))

California: a clause requiring assignment of an invention developed entirely on the employee's own time without the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secrets does not apply, unless the invention relates to the employer's business or actual or demonstrably anticipated research, or results from work done for the employer; a clause that reaches further is unenforceable (Labor Code § 2870)
California: the employer must give the employee written notice of that limit at the time the agreement is made (Labor Code § 2872)
Several other states have similar invention-assignment laws; they were not checked here, so state-specific exhibits need counsel review

Separate from all of this: the SF 312 is an agreement between the government and a person found eligible for classified access, signed before a witness before access is granted and sent to the government (32 CFR 117.10(g))

rules.title: Export-Control Check After an Offer
rules.summary: For a role that works with export-controlled technology (under the ITAR or the EAR), the company needs to know whether the new hire is a U.S. person: a U.S. citizen or national, lawful permanent resident, refugee or asylee. If not, it may need a licence from the State Department (ITAR) or the Commerce Department (EAR) before releasing controlled technical data, because releasing it to a foreign person inside the U.S. counts as an export. The Justice Department's guidance: the ITAR and the EAR contain no hiring requirements, so do not limit jobs to U.S. citizens because of them; assess only the workers whose jobs need it, tell them why, and keep the assessment separate from Form I-9. No rule found sets when the check happens; doing it after an offer, apart from the I-9, keeps citizenship documents out of the hiring decision. Restricted-party screening against the Consolidated Screening List is a related, common step. A security clearance has a different, stricter rule: U.S. citizenship (see clearance-citizenship).
keyPoints: U.S. persons include U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents, and people granted refugee status or asylum (DOJ fact sheet; see itar-us-person)

Releasing technical data to a foreign person in the U.S. is a "deemed export" to every country where that person holds or held citizenship or holds permanent residency (22 CFR 120.50(a)(2), (b)); authorisation comes from the State Department's DDTC or the Commerce Department's BIS, depending on the item (DOJ fact sheet)

Employers with more than three employees may not discriminate in hiring based on national origin, or based on citizenship status against U.S. citizens, nationals, permanent residents, refugees or asylees (with some limits), unless it is required to comply with a law, regulation, executive order or government contract (8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1)-(3)); the DOJ says the ITAR and the EAR impose no such requirement

DOJ best practices: do the assessment only for workers whose positions need export-controlled items; tell them it is to decide whether export authorisation is needed; keep it separate from Form I-9; do not require I-9 documents that prove status; store export documents apart from the I-9; never tell applicants that export rules require a particular citizenship

Restricted-party screening: the Consolidated Screening List combines export screening lists of the Departments of Commerce, State and the Treasury, with a free search engine and API; dealings with a listed party can be prohibited (for example, the Denied Persons List). The page sets no rule about screening employees: screening a new hire is common practice, not a stated hiring rule

Timing is practice, not a rule: the DOJ fact sheet does not say when to assess. Assessing after the offer is accepted means citizenship or immigration documents are never collected before a hiring decision
